The house style for figures: one theme with its colors, shapes and line types, readable labels, and one way to save a figure at its printed size. The file is copied unchanged from the maintainer's [COHERO analysis](https://github.com/VagishHemmige/COHERO-RCT-analysis), so figures look the same across his projects.

::: {.Rcode title="Source code"}
The full R script is available at:

-   [`R/plot_style.R`](https://github.com/VagishHemmige/Fiorica-cryptoccoccus-analysis/blob/main/R/plot_style.R)

It is used by [`R/figures.R`](figures.qmd). The code sections below are imported directly from that script when this page is rendered.
:::

```{r}
#| include: false
#| eval: true
#| cache: false
knitr::read_chunk("../R/plot_style.R")
```

## Check the ggplot2 version

The theme relies on features added in [{ggplot2}](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/) 4.0.0: a theme can carry the palettes its figures use, and labels can be looked up by variable name. On an older version the script stops with a message saying what to update, rather than failing later with a less helpful error.

```{r}
#| label: check-ggplot2-version
#| eval: false
```

## Palettes

A palette is the ordered set of colors (or shapes, or line types) given to the groups in a figure. The colors are the Okabe-Ito set, chosen to stay distinguishable for people with the common kinds of color-vision deficiency, with a neutral dark gray first for a reference group. Groups also differ by point shape and line type, so a figure still works in grayscale and never relies on color alone. This study's figures each show a single series, which takes the first color after the gray.

```{r}
#| label: publication-palettes
#| eval: false
```

## The publication theme

A theme controls everything in a figure that is not data: background, gridlines, text sizes, legend position. `theme_publication()` keeps only what helps a reader: light horizontal gridlines to read values against, thin axis lines, no panel border. It also carries the palettes above, so a figure needs no color settings of its own. Text sizes are set for the printed figure (9 points by default), so a figure should be saved at the size it will be printed.

**Used in the analysis:** Figures: [settings for every figure](figures.qmd); Figures: [Figure 2: survival](figures.qmd#figure-2-survival).

```{r}
#| label: theme-publication
#| eval: false
```

## Labels

`label_figure()` replaces column names with readable names, and `figure_label()` looks up one name for a title or axis label. Both take the labels as arguments, so the file reads nothing from the rest of the project. This study's figures take their readable names from `report_labels`, defined on the [Tables](tables.qmd) page.

```{r}
#| label: label-figure
#| eval: false
```

## Saving a figure

`save_figure()` writes a figure at its printed size in millimetres, in each format needed: PDF and SVG, which keep lines and text sharp at any zoom, for journals; and PNG for the website. Figures 2 and 3 are saved with it.

**Used in the analysis:** Figures: [Figure 2: survival](figures.qmd#figure-2-survival); Figures: [Figure 3: odds ratios](figures.qmd#figure-3-odds-ratios).

```{r}
#| label: save-figure
#| eval: false
```

## The default theme

Loading this file changes no settings. [Figures](figures.qmd) sets `theme_publication()` as the default theme for this project.
